text:
Observing M. de Croisenois with the stern eye of misfortune, Julien noticed the extreme influence that this amiable and good young man attributed to hidden causes. It went so far that he would grow sad and ill-tempered if he saw a somewhat important event ascribed to a simple and entirely natural cause. There is the beginning of madness in that, Julien said to himself. This character bears a striking resemblance to that of the Emperor Alexander, as Prince Korasoff described him to me. During the first year of his stay in Paris, poor Julien, fresh from the seminary and dazzled by the graces, so new to him, of all these amiable young men, had been able only to admire them. Their true character was only just beginning to take shape before his eyes.

I am playing an unworthy role here, he suddenly thought. The matter was to leave his little straw chair in a manner that was not too awkward. He tried to invent something; he was asking something new of an imagination wholly occupied elsewhere. He had to resort to memory; his own was, it must be confessed, rather poor in resources of this kind. The poor boy still had very little experience, and so he was perfectly awkward, in a way noticed by everyone, when he rose to leave the drawing room. His unhappiness was all too evident in his whole manner of being. For three quarters of an hour he had been playing the role of an importunate subordinate from whom no one takes the trouble to conceal what one thinks of him.

The critical observations he had just made about his rivals nevertheless kept him from taking his unhappiness too tragically; to sustain his pride, he had the memory of what had happened the day before yesterday. Whatever their thousand advantages over me, he thought as he entered the garden alone, Mathilde has been for none of them what, twice in my life, she deigned to be for me.

His wisdom went no further. He understood nothing whatever of the character of the singular person whom chance had just made the absolute mistress of all his happiness.

The next day, he confined himself to exhausting both himself and his horse. In the evening he made no further attempt to approach the blue sofa, to which Mathilde remained faithful. He noticed that Count Norbert did not even deign to look at him when they encountered each other in the house. He must be doing himself a strange violence, he thought, he who is naturally so polite.

For Julien, sleep would have been happiness. In spite of his physical fatigue, memories that were all too alluring were beginning to invade his entire imagination. He did not have the insight to see that, by means of his long rides in the woods around Paris, acting only upon himself and not at all upon Mathilde’s heart or mind, he was leaving the disposition of his fate to chance.

It seemed to him that one thing would bring infinite relief to his pain: it would be to speak to Mathilde. But what, however, would he dare say to her?

That was what he was pondering deeply one morning at seven o’clock when, all at once, he saw her enter the library.

“I know, monsieur, that you wish to speak to me.”

“Great God! Who told you?”

“I know it; what does it matter to you? If you have no honor, you can ruin me, or at least attempt to; but this danger, which I do not believe to be real, will certainly not prevent me from being sincere. I no longer love you, monsieur; my foolish imagination deceived me...”

At this terrible blow, distraught with love and unhappiness, Julien tried to justify himself. Nothing could have been more absurd. Does one justify oneself for being displeasing? But reason no longer had any sway over his actions. A blind instinct drove him to postpone the decision of his fate. It seemed to him that as long as he was speaking, everything was not over. Mathilde did not listen to his words; the sound of them irritated her, and she could not conceive that he had the audacity to interrupt her.

The remorse of virtue and that of pride made her equally unhappy that morning. She was in some sense crushed by the dreadful idea of having given rights over her to a little abbé, the son of a peasant. It is almost, she told herself in moments when she exaggerated her unhappiness, as though I had to reproach myself for a weakness for one of the footmen.

In bold and proud characters, there is only one step from anger against oneself to rage against others; in such a case, transports of fury are a keen pleasure.

In an instant, Mademoiselle de La Mole reached the point of overwhelming Julien with the most extreme marks of contempt. She had infinite wit, and that wit triumphed in the art of torturing people’s self-esteem and inflicting cruel wounds upon it.

For the first time in his life, Julien found himself subjected to the action of a superior mind animated against him by the most violent hatred. Far from thinking in the least of defending himself at that moment, his changeable imagination came to despise itself. Hearing himself overwhelmed by such cruel marks of contempt, calculated with so much wit to destroy every good opinion he might have of himself, it seemed to him that Mathilde was right and that she did not say enough.

As for her, she found a delicious pleasure of pride in thus punishing herself and him for the adoration she had felt a few days earlier.

She had no need to invent and think for the first time of the cruel things she addressed to him with such complacency. She was merely repeating what, for the past week, the advocate of the party opposed to love had been saying in her heart.

Every word increased Julien’s dreadful unhappiness a hundredfold. He tried to flee; Mademoiselle de La Mole held him back by the arm with authority.

“Deign to observe,” he said to her, “that you are speaking very loudly; you will be heard from the next room.”

“What does it matter!” Mademoiselle de La Mole replied proudly. “Who will dare say that I am being heard? I intend to cure your petty self-esteem forever of the notions it may have imagined about me.”

When Julien was able to leave the library, he was so astonished that he felt his unhappiness less. Well! She no longer loves me, he kept repeating to himself, speaking aloud as though to teach himself his position. It seems that she loved me for eight or ten days, and I shall love her all my life.

Can it really be possible? She was nothing, nothing to my heart, only a few days ago!

The pleasures of pride flooded Mathilde’s heart; so she had been able to break with him forever! To triumph so completely over so powerful an inclination would make her perfectly happy. Thus this little monsieur will understand, once and for all, that he has and never will have any power over me. She was so happy that at that moment she truly no longer felt any love.
